claims.text: Lightweight high-entropy alloys can combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation stability.
Targeted alloying can induce significant lattice distortion in lightweight high-entropy alloys.
Targeted alloying can promote in situ formation of a uniform, adherent protective oxide layer.
Lattice distortion strengthens the alloy by impeding dislocation motion.
Slower atomic diffusion retards corrosion and oxidation.
A stabilized protective oxide film limits surface degradation at high temperatures.
Controlled cooling or heat treatment can enhance atomic-size mismatch and produce a more uniform distribution of alloying elements.
A uniform distribution of selected alloying elements favors both lattice distortion and continuous protective-oxide formation during annealing.
The proposed treatment will produce enhanced bulk lattice distortion.
The proposed treatment will produce a continuous, coherent, low-density protective surface oxide.
Oxide enrichment in high oxygen-affinity elements passivates the surface against corrosion and high-temperature oxidation.
The treated alloy will have higher yield strength than the baseline alloy.
The treated alloy may have greater creep resistance than the baseline alloy.
The increase in strength will occur without sacrificing corrosion or high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Excessive secondary-phase precipitation, including brittle intermetallic formation, can cause the proposed mechanism to fail.
The proposed mechanism can fail when operating temperature exceeds the stability range of the protective oxide.

Failure to obtain a reproducible, statistically significant yield-strength increase of approximately 10% while maintaining comparable or lower corrosion and oxidation rates would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe enhanced lattice distortion and a more uniform oxide film relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.
